title: India Is Now Selling Gasoline to Russia. The World's Energy Map Just Flipped.
excerpt: Ukrainian drone strikes have knocked out 30% of Russia's refining capacity. India — Moscow's biggest crude buyer — is shipping finished fuel back.
body:
For three years, India has been the world's most enthusiastic buyer of Russian crude oil — snapping up discounted barrels that European customers refused to touch. Now the trade has come full circle. India is shipping refined gasoline back to Russia.

At least 60,000 metric tons of gasoline — roughly 510,000 barrels — have been dispatched from Indian ports aboard two tankers bound for Russia, according to industry sources cited by Reuters. It is the first known seaborne shipment of finished fuel from India to Russia, and it marks an extraordinary reversal in an energy relationship that has defined global commodity markets since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

## Ukraine's Refinery War

The reason Russia needs Indian gasoline is straightforward: Ukraine has systematically dismantled Russia's ability to refine its own oil.

Sustained drone strikes have knocked roughly 30 percent of Russia's oil refining capacity offline, pushing domestic refining throughput to a 21-year low. The damage has come during peak summer driving season, when gasoline consumption in Russia exceeds 110,000 metric tons per day.

The shortfall is acute. Moscow faces a daily deficit of approximately 25,000 tons of gasoline — about 212,500 barrels — that its remaining refineries cannot fill. President Vladimir Putin acknowledged on Sunday that Ukrainian strikes on "critical infrastructure" had created fuel shortages across the country, a rare public admission from the Kremlin.

The consequences on the ground have been severe. Videos from multiple Russian regions show long queues at petrol stations, angry motorists, and in some cases, physical altercations. In the Zabaikalsky region bordering China, authorities have cancelled bus routes and suspended waste collection services, citing fuel constraints. Russia's parliament last week approved emergency tax amendments offering subsidies for fuel imports, explicitly pegged to Indian delivery costs and port prices.


## The Refining Arbitrage

India's role as Russia's fuel supplier is less surprising than it sounds. Indian refiners imported a record 2.7 million barrels per day of Russian crude in June — more than half of India's total oil imports and a record high by any measure. Those refineries, including the world's largest at Jamnagar, have ample capacity to process the crude into gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel.

The arithmetic is simple: India buys Russian crude at a discount, refines it at some of the world's most efficient facilities, and sells the finished product wherever demand is highest. Until now, much of that refined output went to Europe and Southeast Asia. Russia's domestic crisis has opened a new, lucrative market.

The Kremlin plans to import 400,000 metric tons of gasoline monthly from multiple countries, including India and Belarus, which has already tripled its gasoline rail deliveries to Russia. But Belarus and Kazakhstan lack the spare refining capacity to resolve the crisis on their own. India, with its massive and underutilised refining infrastructure, is uniquely positioned to fill the gap.

## The Geopolitical Irony

The circular trade underscores a remarkable geopolitical irony. When Western nations sanctioned Russian energy exports after the 2022 invasion, India became Moscow's economic lifeline, absorbing crude oil that Europe would no longer buy. Indian officials argued the purchases served national interest — energy security at discounted prices.

Now that same crude, processed through Indian refineries, is flowing back to Russia as finished fuel — helping sustain the very war machine that created the sanctions regime in the first place. The arrangement tests the boundaries of India's carefully maintained neutrality in the conflict.

Russia's fuel crisis has also exposed a structural vulnerability that goes beyond this war. Decades of underinvestment in refining infrastructure, combined with the concentration of facilities within drone range of Ukraine, have left the world's third-largest oil producer unable to keep its own petrol stations supplied.

## What It Means for India

For India, the gasoline exports represent a small but symbolically important milestone. The country has spent decades building refining capacity that far exceeds domestic demand, betting that the world would eventually need Indian refineries to process crude into usable fuel.

That bet is paying off. India now operates approximately 5.8 million barrels per day of refining capacity — enough to process its own crude imports and still have surplus to export. The Russia trade adds a new customer to an export portfolio that already includes Europe, Africa, and Southeast Asia.

The risk, as analysts note, is reputational. India's refined fuel exports to Russia could draw scrutiny from Western governments that have tried to cap the value Moscow extracts from its oil exports. So far, there is no indication that the gasoline shipments violate any existing sanctions — Russia is not barred from importing refined products — but the optics of India fuelling Russia's domestic economy while it wages war in Ukraine are unlikely to escape notice.

For now, India appears content to let the market work. No Indian refiner has been publicly identified as the supplier, and neither India's oil ministry nor Russia's energy ministry has commented on the shipments. The tankers, like much of India's Russia trade, move quietly — reshaping global energy flows one cargo at a time.
